payload.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=mechanisms+by+which+accumulated+memory+sequences+induce+distinct+preference+structures+in+autonomous+agents&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Tumour-associated dsRNA accumulation and innate immune activation: mechanistic basis and therapeutic strategies.\", \"abstract\": \"Endogenous double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) links disrupted RNA homoeostasis in cancer to innate immunity. Tumour-associated dsRNA arises from complementary repeat transcripts, mitochondrial transcriptional imbalance, defective RNA processing and cellular stress. Its immunogenicity depends on ligand structure, editing, persistence, localisation, sensor access and pathway competence. ADAR1 and RNA-binding or decay factors buffer self-dsRNA, allowing tumour cells to tolerate potentially immunogenic RNA. Disruption of this control engages RIG-I-MAVS, MDA5-MAVS, TLR3-TRIF, PKR-eIF2α, and OAS-RNase L pathways; Z-conformation RNA can activate ZBP1. Outputs include interferon responses, translational arrest, RNA degradation, and regulated cell death, which can promote antigen presentation and immune-cell recruitment or drive chronic interferon adaptation, suppressive inflammation and treatment resistance. This Review examines critical-target and cumulative-burden models, methods for ligand identification, biomarker-guided patient selection and therapeutic strategies based on viral mimicry, ADAR1 targeting, engineered dsRNA agonists, and delivery platforms.\", \"doi\": \"10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106493\", \"pmid\": \"42800308\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13638791\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106493\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13638791\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13638791?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Exploring and Targeting the Connection of Iron and Copper Homeostasis to Neurodegenerative Diseases.\", \"abstract\": \"Iron (Fe) and copper (Cu) are vital micronutrients that regulate many critical physiological processes in the human body, with their homeostasis in the central nervous system (CNS) being essential for proper neuronal function. Disruptions in their metabolism and regulatory pathways have been associated with the pathogenesis of various forms of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). Despite growing research on metal homeostasis, the intricate molecular mechanisms that link iron and copper metabolism to the initiation and progression of NDDs remain insufficiently elucidated. In this review, we provide a systematic overview of the metabolic processes of iron and copper in the body and CNS, highlighting their interactions with many metal-binding proteins, including transporters, storage proteins, and important intrinsically disordered proteins (e.g., amyloid β-protein, tau, and alpha-synuclein) involved in NDDs. We further dissect the downstream effects of metal ion dyshomeostasis on cellular redox balance, neuroinflammation, autophagy, organelle interaction network, and cell death. Additionally, we discuss current therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting iron and copper dyshomeostasis, as well as the emerging role of artificial intelligence in this field of research. By integrating metal metabolism, metal-protein interactions, the effect of metal dyshomeostasis on downstream biological processes, and potential intervention strategies, this review serves as a comprehensive reference for understanding the pathogenesis of NDDs and offers new perspectives for developing effective therapeutics. Overall, this review underscores the significance of reinstating metal balance for the treatment of neurodegeneration.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/mco2.70766\", \"pmid\": \"42164658\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13183828\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/mco2.70766\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13183828\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13183828?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Rewiring immunity in rheumatoid arthritis: metabolic and epigenetic therapeutic strategies.\", \"abstract\": \"Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease marked by chronic inflammation and destruction of joints and surrounding soft tissues. The pathogenesis of RA is heavily driven by two intertwined and mutually regulatory processes: metabolic reprogramming and epigenetic remodeling. Recent advances reveal a crucial crosstalk wherein metabolic intermediates derived from immune cells act as substrates or cofactors for chromatin-modifying enzymes. This interplay profoundly shapes epigenetic landscapes, thereby exacerbating inflammatory responses and disease progression. Here, we review the mechanisms underlying immune cell metabolic reprogramming in RA and critically examine how metabolite-mediated epigenetic remodeling orchestrates disease pathology. Furthermore, we summarize state-of-the-art epigenetic-targeted therapeutic strategies, offering new insights and a solid theoretical basis for treating RA through the metabolic-epigenetic axis.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fphar.2026.1894277\", \"pmid\": \"42614729\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13482459\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1894277\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13482459\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13482459?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Intelligent immunotherapy: AI-driven optimization of CAR-T therapy in hematologic malignancies.\", \"abstract\": \"Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed outcomes in selected hematologic malignancies, yet its delivery remains constrained by variable efficacy, acute and prolonged toxicities, and complex manufacturing logistics. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied across the CAR-T continuum at three distinct levels of evidentiary maturity. Externally validated parsimonious models built on routine clinical and laboratory data including CAR-HEMATOTOX, endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) and m-EASIX, MyCARe, and gradient-boosting cytokine release syndrome predictors provide deployable risk stratification today. Methodologically sophisticated tools using deep-learning positron emission tomography (PET) segmentation, attention-based digital-pathology analysis, and multimodal fusion of imaging with laboratory and circulating tumor DNA features have demonstrated technical promise but generally lack the multi-center external validation required for clinical-grade deployment. Forward-looking applications, including digital-twin frameworks, large language models, and closed-loop adaptive therapy, remain at the prototype stage and have not yet been validated for CAR-T. This review synthesizes these three tiers, summarizes 18 published AI and statistical-modeling tools in a comparative performance table, and compares data characteristics and AI modeling paradigms across large B cell lymphoma, B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and multiple myeloma. We also identify the implementation realities-absent regulatory clearance, demographic and racial bias in training data, and post-deployment model drift-that condition the field's evolution. The contribution of AI to CAR-T therapy, as the evidence currently stands, is the calibrated quantification of established risk factors rather than the discovery of novel biology, but the methodological and data infrastructure foundations are now in place for the broader transformation that the next decade may enable.\", \"doi\": \"10.1016/j.isci.2026.117255\", \"pmid\": \"42904142\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13682363\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117255\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13682363\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13682363?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "98c6a72b473219cdbe548be66047f6dbefd6ddb8891b764564e73bfc54e740b0", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "memory_formed_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106493", "doi:10.1002/mco2.70766", "doi:10.3389/fphar.2026.1894277", "doi:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117255", "pmc:PMC13638791", "pmc:PMC13183828", "pmc:PMC13482459", "pmc:PMC13682363"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106493", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13638791", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13638791?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1002/mco2.70766", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13183828", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13183828?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1894277", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13482459"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=computational+frameworks+for+automated+axiom+falsification+in+autonomous+systems&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.4018/979-8-2600-0413-5.ch003\", \"title\": [\"The Proliferation of Autonomous Cyber Weapons?\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Autonomous cyber weapons mark a major shift in digital conflict by compressing the cycle of observation, analysis, decision, and action while expanding the scale of possible offensive effects. This chapter examines their proliferation as a socio-technical and strategic phenomenon rather than a technical programming issue. It defines autonomous cyber weapons as systems able to sense digital environments, reason over goals and constraints, choose among actions, and execute bounded cyber effects with limited or delayed human intervention. Drawing on scholarship in cybersecurity, adversarial machine learning, cyber conflict, and ethics, the chapter proposes a layered framework showing how data pipelines, knowledge graphs, model-based reasoning, action selection, and feedback loops can form offensive agentic. It also explains how these systems may intensify asymmetric warfare by reducing labor demands, accelerating operations, lowering coordination costs, and supporting continual adaptation, then concludes with governance, oversight, testing, escalation control, and resilient defense.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-0413-5.ch003\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 29]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.22399/ijcesen.5196\", \"title\": [\"Agentic AI Frameworks: Building Autonomous, Self-Healing Systems for Financial Infrastructure\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Financial infrastructure management is facing unprecedented challenges as distributed architectures with hundreds of interdependent microservices impose complexity beyond the human cognitive limit for real-time monitoring and intervention. Conventional reactive monitoring systems bring intolerable latency between anomaly discovery and human perception, and the manual diagnostic processes take considerable time during which the services are degraded. Security alert proliferation overloads operations teams, with false positives above 90% in expert domains like anti-money laundering surveillance. Agentic AI frameworks overcome these inherent limitations with self-contained systems that combine perception, reasoning, and action capabilities within operational infrastructure cores. Multi-agent architectures provide specialist domain expertise in areas of network performance, database optimization, security threat response, and capacity management while retaining collaborative problem-solving abilities for sophisticated failure scenarios. Self-restoration mechanisms utilize predictive analysis to determine precursors to failure minutes to hours in advance of full service loss, allowing for preventive actions that do not impact customers at all. Automated threat identification and response condense incident containment windows from hours to seconds, significantly shrinking vulnerability windows that advanced attackers target. Immutable audit trails using blockchain technologies meet regulatory demands for operational visibility while smart contract execution ensures policy compliance. Explainability issues call for the creation of understandable decision models that can explain reasoning logic in a human-readable form. Trust calibration needs graduated autonomy models that move from advisory recommendations to supervised execution toward complete autonomy for routine situations. Directions for the future include federated learning that facilitates cross-institutional sharing of knowledge, sophisticated causal modeling to predict intervention cascades, and digital twin incorporation, offering safe test beds.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.22399/ijcesen.5196\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 12, 29]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6316538\", \"title\": [\"A Security-Focused Study on Automated Threat Intelligence and Risks of Autonomous Agentic AI Frameworks&nbsp;\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Cybersecurity threats are increasing rapidly in both scale and sophistication. Threat intelligence plays a crucial role in identifying vulnerabilities, exploits, and emerging attack patterns. However, manual collection of threat intelligence from open platforms such as social media, security forums, and vulnerability databases is inefficient and error-prone, especially for students and early researchers. This paper presents a study on automated threat intelligence collection using open-source information while simultaneously assessing the security risks introduced by modern autonomous \\\"agentic AI\\\" frameworks. A detailed security analysis of an agentic framework commonly known as Open Claude (also referred to as Open Claw or Moltabot) is conducted to demonstrate how improper autonomy, lack of sandboxing, and uncontrolled third-party instruction execution can result in severe system compromise. The paper proposes a safer, restricted automation model and provides mitigation recommendations suitable for educational and research environments.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6316538\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/cbo9781316597873.013\", \"title\": [\"Autonomous weapons systems: new frameworks for individual responsibility\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781316597873.013\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1920, 12, 31]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "37f8f5dee5788decf41ae1bd6d906d0e39269ba26d377a8764c48590b7f8b236", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0413-5.ch003", "doi:10.22399/ijcesen.5196", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6316538", "doi:10.1017/cbo9781316597873.013"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-0413-5.ch003", "https://doi.org/10.22399/ijcesen.5196", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6316538", "https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781316597873.013"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=automated+methods+for+identifying+reasoning+blind+spots+through+causal+model+introspection&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1079/9781800620575.0009\", \"title\": [\"Identifying the causal agent of leaf spots and blights\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1079/9781800620575.0009\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023, 7, 30]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1002/9781119209010.ch2\", \"title\": [\"A Model of Blind Spots, Learning and Change\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119209010.ch2\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2012, 1, 2]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21203/rs.3.rs-6866975/v1\", \"title\": [\"REACTOR: Reliability Engineering with Automated Causal Tracking and Observability Reasoning\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n

Reliability engineering aims to ensure that systems perform as expected over time, yet it faces various challenges in identifying and mitigating potential failures. We introduce REACTOR, an advanced framework prioritizing automated causal tracking and observability reasoning to improve reliability analysis. REACTOR uniquely utilizes a dual-layer architecture to facilitate the identification of failure sources through thorough causal analysis and subsequently assesses the ramifications of these failures on system performance through observability reasoning. This framework minimizes reliance on manual interventions, enabling users to achieve a deeper understanding of the reliability of complex systems. We employ sophisticated machine learning techniques to bolster the detection of anomalies and pinpoint their root causes, fostering a proactive approach to reliability management.
